summary: This standards-track memo explains how to use DNSSEC digital signatures on update requests so that dynamic DNS changes are limited to parties holding the right keys. It was replaced by RFC 3007.

eli5.summary: Only someone holding the right signature stamp can change the phone book.

subtitle: Using digital signatures to control who can change DNS data dynamically.

tldr.problem: DNS Dynamic Update allows administrators to add or change DNS records in real time, but without security, anyone could change the records to redirect traffic or disable services.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC combines DNS dynamic update with DNSSEC digital signatures: update requests and the new data are signed with cryptographic keys, and the DNS server verifies the signature before accepting the change.
tldr.outcome: Only holders of the correct private keys can change DNS records, allowing dynamic updates in a secure zone. It was later replaced by RFC 3007 which simplified the approach.

facts.value: Defined by owner name and class

today: RFC 2137 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 3007. RFC 3007 provides a simplified secure dynamic update mechanism.

sections.title: Dynamic DNS With Security
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) maps domain names to IP addresses. RFC 2136 added dynamic update, allowing administrators to change DNS records without manually editing zone files and restarting the server. However, RFC 2136 did not describe how to secure these updates.

This RFC adds security using DNSSEC digital signatures. It specifies how to authenticate update requests using request signatures and how to authenticate the resulting data using data signatures. The requester must possess a private key authorized for the names being updated, and the DNS server verifies the signature on the request before making any changes.
sections.eli5: When you ask the DNS server to change the phone book, you sign your request. The server checks your signature to make sure you are allowed to make that change.

sections.title: Keys and Authorization
sections.content:
Dynamic updates are controlled by update keys stored in the DNS as KEY resource records. Each update key has a scope defined by its owner name and class. A key can authorize updates to records with the same owner name, or to any name matching a wildcard key (including specific names that fall within the wildcard's scope).

The KEY record includes a four-bit signatory field with flags controlling what the key can update. The zone control bit authorizes changes to zone structure (NS records, glue A records, zone KEY records). The strong update bit allows the key to modify records even if other records with the same name are controlled by different keys. The unique name update bit restricts the key to managing only one name at a time, limiting how many names a key can flood into the zone. The general update bit is used when the other three bits are zero, to mark a key as an update key.
sections.eli5: Each key has permission flags controlling what it can change: whether it can change the zone structure, whether it can override other keys, and whether it can create many new names.

sections.title: Mode A (Offline) and Mode B (Online)
sections.content:
The RFC defines two operational modes, distinguished by whether the zone's private key is kept offline or online. Mode A keeps the zone key offline for maximum security of static data. Dynamic updates are signed by update keys and stored separately. The server only verifies signatures, which is fast, but dynamic data is less secure and cannot be zone-transferred securely since only update keys signed the dynamic records.

Mode B keeps the zone key online. When an authenticated update succeeds, the server signs the new data with the zone key. This makes dynamic data as secure as static data and allows secure zone transfer, but the server must perform cryptographic signing, which is computationally expensive. If the server is compromised, an attacker can sign false data with the zone key.
sections.eli5: Mode A: keep the master key locked in a safe and only check signatures from updaters (fast, but changes are less protected). Mode B: keep the master key online and re-sign everything with it (safe but slow).

sections.title: Request and Data Signatures
sections.content:
Request signatures are required for all updates. They are SIG resource records placed at the end of the update request, in the Additional information section. Each request signature covers the entire request (DNS header and all data) using a key authorized for the names being updated. If an update affects multiple names covered by different keys, the requester must provide request signatures for each key.

In Mode A, data signatures are also required. These are SIG records that will be added to the zone along with the new data, signing it with the update key. In Mode B, data signatures are not needed because the server will sign all zone data with the zone key.
sections.eli5: You sign the entire update request to prove you are authorized. In Mode A, you also provide signatures for the data so it stays signed. In Mode B, the server signs everything itself.

sections.title: Security Trade-Offs
sections.content:
Any zone permitting dynamic updates is less secure than a static zone maintained offline. At minimum, secure dynamic update requires the zone SOA record to be online and changeable so that the serial number can be incremented when updates occur. If the DNS server is compromised, an attacker with access to the SOA's private key could change the serial number arbitrarily.

To contain the damage, administrators can isolate dynamic records in separate subzones. A main zone can remain static and offline in Mode A, while dynamic subzones operate in Mode B. This limits the impact of a compromise to just the dynamic zones.
sections.eli5: Once you allow changes to the zone, you have to keep the signing key online and vulnerable. The best you can do is keep important zones locked down and let only less critical zones change dynamically.
